title: Breath with a word
hookLine: many traditions pair breath with words (the Jesus Prayer, dhikr, mantra); here we use a plain one, "here"

cards: In the 1880s, a little book was printed in Russia about a man with no home and one question. He had heard a line from Paul's letter, pray without ceasing, and he wanted to know how anyone could do that.
He walked from town to town asking. At last an old monk gave him a short prayer and taught him to let it ride on his breath and his heartbeat, until it went on under everything he did.
The book is called The Way of a Pilgrim, and nobody knows for sure who wrote it. But the idea in it is very old, and it turns up in many places.

teach.h: THE JESUS PRAYER, ON THE BREATH.
teach.b: Three homes, one at a time, each keeping its own meaning. In Eastern Orthodox Christianity, the prayer the pilgrim learned is the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me.

Monks of Mount Athos and many lay Orthodox Christians have said it for centuries, some saying the first half on the in-breath and the second half on the out-breath. For them it is a prayer to Christ, not a technique.
In Islam there is dhikr, remembrance: short phrases in praise of God, repeated, often on prayer beads, and in some Sufi circles sung together with the rhythm of the breath.
For those who say it, it is remembering God, not a calming exercise.

In Hindu and Buddhist practice there is mantra: a sacred sound or phrase repeated aloud or silently, sometimes timed to the breath. Each tradition would say its words matter, in its own way. What they share is a shape.
The mind wanders easily on the breath alone.
Give it a word to carry, and the word becomes a handrail. This path doesn't borrow anyone's prayer, or dress one up as a technique.
It uses a plain word that belongs to everyone and claims nothing: here. Breathing in, here. Breathing out, here.
It's a reminder, not a prayer: it says where you are and when. And if you already pray with words of your own tradition, those are there for you to use.

how: Eastern Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a prayer rope and sometimes with the breath; Muslims practice dhikr, repeated remembrance of God; Hindus and Buddhists repeat mantras. Each keeps its own meaning, and on this path a plain word like "here" is used as a reminder, not a prayer.

games.why: he walks and asks, until an old monk teaches him a short prayer that rides on the breath.

practice: Let the breath find its own pace, and say silently here on the in-breath and here on the out-breath, ten times, slowly; when your mind wanders, take hold of the word again, like a handrail.
If you pray, and your tradition has its own words for this, you can use those instead. After ten, let the word go and sit in the quiet it leaves.

wordCard.voice: Mantra. A word carried on the breath, a handrail for a wandering mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from the Orthodox Christian tradition: stillness, quiet. Those who pray the Jesus Prayer in stillness are called hesychasts.

carryVoice: Your line: here. One small word, and the shortest way back to where you are. Until tomorrow.
